title: Police & Law Enforcement
tagline: Patrol, investigations, and rank — the dedicated law-enforcement career path.
summary: A deep-dive specialization of the Public Safety roadmap: the law-enforcement career from written exam and POST academy through patrol, investigations, specialty units, and rank — plus the professional standards that shape it.

sources.label: O*NET — Police and Sheriff's Patrol Officers (33-3051.00)

detail.description: Law-enforcement hiring runs written exam → physical test → oral board → background investigation → medical/psychological → academy → field training, often over a year.
detail.why: Understanding the full pipeline — and staying patient and documented through it — is the first professional skill.
learn: Map the process for three target agencies
Assemble a complete background file early
Prepare for each stage deliberately
Apply broadly and track deadlines

detail.description: The police academy (typically ~6 months) covers criminal law, traffic law, tactics, driving, fitness, and scenario training to state POST-style standards.
detail.why: Academy success is trainable — fitness, study discipline, and stress tolerance are buildable before day one.
learn: Train past the academy's fitness standards
Build note systems for high-volume legal content
Practice scenario decisions aloud
Learn the FTO phase structure ahead

detail.description: The Field Training Officer phase pairs recruits with veteran officers for months of evaluated real calls — daily observation reports decide probation.
detail.why: FTO is where academy knowledge meets street reality; coachability is the trait FTOs grade hardest.
learn: Own your daily observation reports
Ask for honest feedback at every shift end
Practice report writing until drafts need no edits
Learn your beat's geography cold

resources.title: O*NET — Police and Sheriff's Patrol Officers

tasks: Patrol assigned areas, respond to calls, enforce laws, and prepare case reports for prosecution.

detail.description: Patrol work: proactive presence, calls for service, traffic enforcement, de-escalation, arrests, and the judgment calls that define modern policing.
detail.why: Patrol is the profession's foundation — every specialty unit recruits from strong patrol performance.
learn: Master the traffic-stop routine and officer safety
Learn de-escalation and proportionate response
Write reports that survive court scrutiny
Know your use-of-force policy thoroughly

detail.description: Reports are evidence: chronological, complete, objective writing — and testimony that survives cross-examination starts with the report.
detail.why: Cases and careers rise or fall on documentation; great reports make great courtroom days.
learn: Practice factual chronological writing weekly
Learn to document force decisions precisely
Observe testimony from the gallery
Get veteran feedback on five drafts

detail.description: Detective work: case screening, interviews and interrogations, warrants, evidence coordination, and working cases to court — selected from strong patrol records.
detail.why: Investigations reward patience and analysis — the classic destination for officers who love casework.
learn: Learn interview vs interrogation frameworks
Practice warrant-affidavit writing
Organize case files for prosecutors
Study one closed case end-to-end

detail.description: Chain of custody is sacred: collection, packaging, labeling, transfer logs, and storage discipline — one gap can destroy a prosecution.
detail.why: Evidence handling is unforgiving and teaches the discipline every specialty requires.
learn: Learn collection and packaging standards per evidence type
Master transfer documentation completely
Practice courtroom-proof custody habits
Audit a mock property room for gaps

detail.description: Specialty assignments: K9, traffic/DUI, narcotics, school resource officers, crisis intervention teams, SWAT selection, and task forces with federal partners.
detail.why: Specialties keep long careers engaged and build skills agencies and employers prize later.
learn: List your agencies' units and selection bars
Build the fitness/skills your target unit tests
Ask unit members what actually gets people selected
Keep a spotless record as the entry ticket

detail.description: Promotions run exams and assessment centers: sergeant (first-line supervision) → lieutenant → captain → command staff — leadership, law, and administration tested throughout.
detail.why: Rank multiplies influence over culture and policy — the profession's leadership path.
learn: Get the promotional reading list years early
Practice supervisory scenario exercises
Learn budget and discipline administration
Track eligibility windows and apply every cycle

detail.description: Federal law enforcement (FBI, DEA, ATF, Marshal's Service, Homeland Security Investigations) hires from academia and from police experience — with its own academies and relocation expectations.
detail.why: Federal careers extend the profession nationally — competitive, well-paid, and selective about records.
learn: Compare federal agencies' missions and entry programs
Note age limits and fitness standards
Keep a spotless record from day one
Learn the federal application rhythm

detail.description: Legitimacy is built in relationships: knowing residents and businesses, transparent communication after incidents, and consistent fair treatment — operationally decisive, not decorative.
detail.why: Cooperation determines whether cases get solved — community trust is an investigative asset.
learn: Introduce yourself on your beat by name
Attend one community meeting per quarter
Learn your city's oversight structure
Follow through visibly on resident concerns

detail.description: The job's exposures — trauma, shifts, hypervigilance — require deliberate sleep, fitness, peer support, and normalizing counseling across a career.
detail.why: Officers who use wellness systems early keep judgment sharp and careers long.
learn: Build a shift-work sleep system
Use peer-support and EAP resources early
Maintain fitness standards without drama
Keep one identity fully outside the badge

detail.description: Officers are held to off-duty standards: social media, associations, finances, and public behavior are all reviewable — character-and-fitness continues after hiring.
detail.why: Most separations trace to off-duty conduct — knowing the rules protects a hard-won career.
learn: Read your agency's conduct policy completely
Audit your online presence like an investigator
Keep finances orderly — checks continue
Disclose and ask when in doubt

detail.description: Ladder: recruit → patrol officer → senior/unit officer → detective or sergeant → lieutenant → command; civilian continuations: federal service, security leadership, investigations, training.
detail.why: The ladder is transparent and pension-backed — planning branches early compounds into options.
learn: Map the ladder and its timelines at your agency
Decide specialist-depth vs leadership-breadth
Build transferable skills from year five
Set a 20-year sketch with checkpoints

detail.description: Post-service branches: security leadership, corporate investigations, emergency management, insurance investigation, and training roles — all valuing sworn experience.
detail.why: Knowing the landing zones makes service careers safer bets and shapes smart specializations.
learn: List post-service roles common in your region
Note certifications private employers value
Build outside networks from year five
Keep a transferable-skills inventory
